name: Periodontal treatment

lead: Periodontal treatment covers everything dentists and periodontists do to control gum disease: cleaning below the gumline, surgery in advanced cases, adjunct antibiotics and regular maintenance visits. The appearance payoff is keeping healthy, attached gums, a stable smile line, your own teeth and fresher breath.

Treatment aims to remove bacterial plaque and calculus, reduce pocket depth and inflammation, and keep plaque under control through home care. Periodontitis is reported to be the main cause of adult tooth loss worldwide, and some randomised trials have examined whether treating it also changes systemic markers, with varying results.

paras: It usually starts with home plaque control and professional cleaning, moves to surgery or local or systemic antibiotics for advanced cases, and continues with ongoing maintenance visits and lifestyle changes.

Surgery and instrumentation carry the usual procedural risks such as soreness and sensitivity. A Cochrane review described evidence that treating gum disease improves conditions like blood pressure as insufficient.

chain: Teeth kept, smile and breath preserved
angle.text: Treating gum disease keeps gums healthy and attached, which preserves the smile line, the teeth themselves and fresher breath. It is well studied for gum disease, and the appearance benefits follow from keeping the gums and teeth intact.

lead: Periodontal treatment is the set of professional and home-care measures used to manage periodontal (gum) disease, which ranges from gingivitis to periodontitis with bone loss and tooth loss. Options include home plaque control, professional root-surface instrumentation, surgery for advanced cases, local or systemic antibiotics, lifestyle changes and ongoing maintenance.[1]

Periodontitis is reported to be the main cause of adult tooth loss worldwide and has been studied for associations with diabetes and cardiovascular disease.[1][2] Some randomised trials have examined whether treating it changes systemic markers, with varying results across outcomes.[3][4]

paras: Encyclopedic sources list brushing at least twice and flossing daily, regular professional cleaning and non-surgical instrumentation below the gumline, surgery where non-surgical therapy is insufficient, local drug delivery such as tetracycline, and systemic antibiotics in some cases, for which evidence of added benefit is low-certainty. Smoking cessation and diet are also discussed.[1] A 2017 review asked how many options exist for one disease, comparing non-surgical and surgical approaches.[5]

An 11-year maintenance study examined how residual pockets influence progression of periodontitis and tooth loss.[6] An earlier five-year study of 100 patients with furcation involvement reported that further destruction in those areas could be arrested after treatment.[7]

Periodontitis is associated with raised inflammatory markers and with diabetes, with a two-way relationship described between the two; many other associations are not proven causal.[1][2] A randomised trial of 120 patients with severe periodontitis compared intensive treatment with community-based care and measured endothelial function and inflammatory markers.[3] A 12-month randomised trial studied systemic effects of periodontitis treatment in type 2 diabetes,[8] and another trial examined periodontal treatment and preterm birth.[9]

Randomised trials have tested periodontal treatment against vascular, diabetic and pregnancy outcomes.[3][8][9] A Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found insufficient evidence that treatment lowers blood pressure.[1] Registered trials include studies of pocket depth change, treatment in diabetes, myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular function.[10][11][12][13] Outcome details beyond the abstracts are not summarised here.

timeline.event: A five-year evaluation of multirooted tooth treatment is published.[7]
A randomised trial of periodontal treatment and preterm birth is published.[9]
A trial of intensive periodontal treatment and endothelial function is published.[3]
A 12-month trial in type 2 diabetes is published.[8]
